profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a multinational company's treasury and pensions function to prepare a board workshop on capital needs across its defined-benefit pension arrangements. The immediate context is that the company has been reviewing recent research on how non-systematic mortality risk falls with pooling, while systematic mortality risk remains material even in larger portfolios, and wants to translate that insight into an internal capital planning memo before the next quarterly board risk session. The agenda is to decide what analysis will be produced, which pension section(s) will be used as examples, how mortality and financial risk will be combined in the work, who owns each piece, and what timeline will support the board pack. The expected outcome is a practical workplan for a short decision memo and supporting sensitivity charts on 'required capital' for the company's smaller and larger pension arrangements.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Longevity modeling, stochastic ALM, pension solvency analysis
members.background: Fellow actuary who previously worked in a life insurer's capital modeling team and now leads internal pension risk analytics for the corporate sponsor.
members.private_state: She wants the board discussion to take systematic mortality seriously rather than over-focusing on pooling, and she wants to reuse the actuarial team's existing modeling framework so the work can be done quickly without reopening methodology debates.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues say 'required capital' in a pensions context, they mean one-year economic capital under the firm's actuarial solvency framework rather than a cash reserve or accounting top-up.
A meaningful pooling analysis counts all scheme members whose liabilities are in the portfolio, including active, deferred, and pensioner lives, not just pensions in payment.
In the current project, 'the smaller plan' obviously refers to the closed Heritage Salaried Section that the actuarial committee flagged last month as having thin mortality experience.
Using the 'existing mortality stress set' means reusing the stochastic longevity model from the last ALM refresh, with financial scenarios already linked to it.

members.name: David Chen
members.role: Director of Treasury and Capital Planning
members.expertise: Corporate funding strategy, board risk packs, capital allocation across legal entities
members.background: Finance leader with a background in corporate treasury and pension funding negotiations, responsible for translating technical risk analysis into board-ready capital planning decisions.
members.private_state: He wants a concise board recommendation that can inform next year's sponsor funding envelope, and he prefers to anchor the analysis in the reporting structures and stress packs already used in finance.
hidden_assumptions: When the team discusses 'required capital' for a pension plan, it means the amount of sponsor-side capital or reserve that may need to be set aside before the next board cycle.
For planning purposes, pooling in mortality risk is mainly about the pensioner population because those lives drive near-term benefit cash flows and board attention.
The 'small plan' in this discussion is naturally the Executive Top-Up Trust, since it is the smallest legal pension vehicle and the one treasury could realistically treat separately.
The 'existing stress set' means the finance ORSA-style stress workbook already used for board materials, not a separate actuarial stochastic calibration.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to estimate the plan's 'required capital' and discuss capital per member.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means economic capital at plan inception or over a one-year solvency horizon under the actuarial risk framework, including mortality and market risk.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the sponsor's practical capital buffer or reserve top-up needed for the next planning cycle and board funding decision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard in both actuarial and finance conversations, and both interpretations plausibly fit a board-planning meeting, so the apparent agreement feels complete.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about testing the insight on 'the smaller plan' first.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the Heritage Salaried Section, a closed section with around 2,300 total members and sparse internal mortality experience.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the Executive Top-Up Trust, a separate legal vehicle with roughly 480 members and a distinct treasury funding line.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each person has a different organizational frame for what counts as the relevant pension unit, but both know there is at least one obviously smaller arrangement, so neither expects ambiguity.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts in the pooling headcount
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to show how the pooling effect changes as 'member numbers' increase.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends member numbers to include active, deferred, and pensioner members because all are part of the liability pool driving non-systematic mortality risk.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends member numbers to mean pensioners in payment, since that is the population most relevant to near-term funding and board capital discussions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Headcount sounds like a straightforward administrative quantity, and both groupings are commonly used in pension work, so the difference hides inside a familiar shorthand.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'using the existing stress set' entails
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use the 'existing stress set' so the work can be done quickly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to reuse the actuarial team's stochastic longevity and market scenario library from the last ALM refresh.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 plans to slot the results into the finance team's standard board stress workbook with its deterministic longevity shock and market stresses.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams routinely describe their own established materials as 'the existing stress set,' and in a planning meeting the phrase sounds like harmless efficiency rather than a modeling choice.
